source.title: Scaling Laws for Emulation of Stellar Spectra

record.file_problem: The full paper, including appendices, is present. Some equations and typesetting are garbled, but the text is readable and not cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests scaling-law behavior in stellar-spectrum emulation and refines its scope, reporting finite-data effects, changes across compute regimes, and sensitivity to model and fitting choices.
record.gate_note: The study measures validation MSE for TransformerPayne spectral emulators, not language-model cross-entropy. Its scaling sweeps and architecture comparisons bear on the listed versions in the spectral-emulation setting. Results cited from other studies, hyperparameter values used to choose configurations, and projected performance for a 1-billion-parameter model are not recorded as measured-result rows.
record.test_reason: The study fits power laws of validation MSE against dataset size, parameters and compute, and fits compute-optimal model and data allocation, for Transformer emulators of synthetic stellar spectra. That is a new setting (non-language regression with MSE) with direct results on the claim's form. It is not a targeted argument that a version is wrong, so T3 fits better than the record's T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that validation MSE follows power laws: L∝D^-1.34, P^-1.21 and C^-0.76 (C^-0.87 sub-epoch). Along the compute frontier they find D∝C^0.38 and P∝C^0.61, so both should grow, with model size faster. Above N≥4, total parameter count rather than shape predicts performance. They project that compute-optimal scaling meets the data-limited ceiling near 3M spectra and ~1B parameters.
record.recipe_differences: This is a spectral-emulator regression study using TransformerPayne, synthetic stellar spectra, and validation MSE, rather than language-model pretraining with cross-entropy. It uses scaling sweeps and compute-frontier fits, but studies a different task, data type, model scale, and loss.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted model-size exponent changes when the largest models are excluded. Compute-frontier behavior differs below versus above approximately 10^17 FLOPs, where training enters the multi-epoch regime. Architecture effects depend on depth: models with fewer than four blocks underperform, and hyperparameter stability degrades at extreme depths.

fits_no_version.finding: Under µP the optimal learning rate stays ~2×10^-3 across widths 64–512 and across token and head changes. Under standard parametrization it shifts ~3x, and with depth µP fails beyond 0.5–2x the proxy depth.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hyperparameter transfer (µP) holds for width but not depth in non-language Transformer regression.

record.problems: The study uses one synthetic plane-parallel LTE dataset and validation MSE rather than downstream inference performance or domain transfer. The compute frontier is restricted to a discrete set of architectures and a limited dataset; above approximately 10^17 FLOPs, repeated examples make the data a constraint. No uncertainty estimates for fitted exponents are stated. The paper notes that models above approximately 10^7 parameters approach the dataset-size limit.
record.rows_left_out: No additional reported scaling or architecture result rows were omitted.

untested.parts: Language-model cross-entropy; the study only tests spectral-emulator MSE.
No out-of-sample check that small-run fits predict much larger runs. The 1B-parameter projection is a forecast, not a test.
Language-model allocation; whether Kaplan or Hoffmann holds for text. Allocation beyond 10^17 FLOPs or with continuous model sizes.
Language models and non-Transformer shapes; architecture ranges beyond d≤256, N≤24.
Image, video, fine-tuning and transfer. Domain transfer is explicitly left for future work.
No downstream task or stellar-parameter inference accuracy is measured.

missing.what: At similar parameter counts, deeper models become unstable sooner than wider ones (54 unstable models). This bears on whether shape matters little.
Abstract allocation numbers (2.5x data, 3.8x model per 10x compute) differ from the body's 2.4x and 4.1x.

record.verdict_notes: The system is a non-language regression Transformer, so V3, V4 and V7 verdicts apply only by analogy, in this setting. All curves are envelopes over discrete sweeps, with no uncertainty on the exponents. The allocation fits exclude the multi-epoch regime by construction. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy of language models as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small language-model runs predict much larger language-model runs.

The study tests an analogous compute-optimal allocation for a spectral emulator, using model parameters and processed spectra rather than language-model parameters and text tokens. It does not test language-model allocation laws.
Architecture effects are tested for TransformerPayne configurations within the explored ranges, not across other model families.

Tests synthetic stellar-spectrum emulation with MSE. It does not test image or video models, fine-tuning, transfer, or other modalities; repeated-example training is examined only as part of the spectral experiments.
Downstream task performance or its relationship to pretraining loss.
The paper reports setup- and fit-dependent effects for its spectral-emulation experiments; it does not assess disagreements between language-model scaling-law studies.

rows.subject: TransformerPayne models (best result for each dataset size; aggregate across architectures and training durations)
rows.operation_detail: Sweep training dataset size and fit best validation MSE at each size

conditions.value: synthetic normalized stellar spectra, plane-parallel LTE

rows.measure: Best validation MSE versus dataset size; fitted exponent −1.34, reported as a 22-fold MSE reduction per 10-fold increase in dataset size
rows.note: The reported curve is an envelope: for each dataset size, the authors select the best result across explored architectures and training durations.

rows.subject: TransformerPayne models (best result for each model size; aggregate across dataset sizes and training durations)
rows.operation_detail: Sweep model parameter count and fit best validation MSE at each size

conditions.value: synthetic normalized stellar spectra, plane-parallel LTE

rows.measure: Best validation MSE versus parameter count; fitted exponent −1.21, reported as a 16-fold MSE reduction per 10-fold increase in parameter count
rows.note: The authors report slight flattening for models above approximately 10^7 parameters, approaching a limit imposed by the 100,000-spectrum dataset.
rows.check: Linkage fine. For V7 the reported flattening above ~10^7 parameters is a bend away from a single power law. The curve is an envelope over dataset sizes and durations.

rows.operation_detail: Refit the model-size scaling curve after excluding the largest models

conditions.value: best validation MSE versus parameter count

rows.measure: Fitted exponent for validation MSE versus parameter count
rows.note: The fitted exponent changes when the largest models are omitted.
rows.check: State should be observed, not partial. V7's effect is that the exponent depends on fit choices, and it does: −1.21 to −1.41 when the two largest models are dropped.

rows.subject: TransformerPayne models (best result for each model size; aggregate across dataset sizes and training durations)
rows.operation_detail: Refit the model-size scaling curve after excluding the largest models

conditions.value: best validation MSE versus parameter count

rows.measure: Fitted exponent for validation MSE versus parameter count
rows.note: The fitted exponent changes further when three of the largest models are omitted.
rows.check: State should be observed. Dropping three models gives −1.54 vs −1.21, a clear fit-range dependence.

rows.subject: TransformerPayne models (compute frontier; aggregate across model configurations)
rows.operation_detail: Fit validation MSE against training compute for frontier models
rows.measure: Compute-frontier validation MSE; fitted exponent −0.76, reported as an approximately 5.7-fold MSE reduction per 10-fold increase in compute
rows.note: The frontier is the lower envelope of results across model sizes. It includes runs that revisit training examples.
rows.check: The all-frontier fit alone does not show fit-dependence; the V7 comparison is carried by r6 and r9. Drop V7.

rows.subject: TransformerPayne models (compute frontier; aggregate across model configurations)
rows.operation_detail: Fit validation MSE against compute on the sub-epoch compute frontier
rows.measure: Compute-frontier validation MSE; fitted exponent −0.87, reported as a 7.4-fold reduction per 10-fold increase in compute
rows.note: The authors restrict this fit to the regime below 10^17 FLOPs, where the training examples have not been revisited.
rows.check: Fine. The exponent is −0.87 in the sub-epoch regime vs −0.76 over all compute, so the fitted exponent depends on the regime included.

rows.subject: TransformerPayne models (compute frontier; aggregate across model configurations)
rows.operation_detail: Fit processed training examples against compute for frontier models
rows.measure: Optimal processed training examples versus compute; fitted exponent 0.38, reported as approximately 2.4-fold more examples per 10-fold increase in compute
rows.note: Processed examples are batch size times training steps; this is not the number of unique spectra in the dataset.
rows.check: Missing a V3 link: this is the data-allocation exponent (D ∝ C^0.38). The V7 link is not supported by this row alone. The abstract gives 2.5-fold, the body 2.4-fold. The quantity is processed spectra, which the authors equate with optimal unique data in the sub-epoch regime.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.4.4; Figure 7 middle panel and caption.

rows.subject: TransformerPayne models (compute frontier; aggregate across model configurations)
rows.operation_detail: Fit parameter count against compute for frontier models
rows.measure: Optimal model parameter count versus compute; fitted exponent 0.61, reported as approximately 4.1-fold larger per 10-fold increase in compute
rows.note: The fit uses a discrete set of tested architectures and is restricted to the sub-epoch regime.
rows.check: Abstract says 3.8-fold per 10x compute; the body says 4.1-fold (exponent 0.61). The fit covers 10 discrete architectures, below 10^17 FLOPs only.

rows.subject: TransformerPayne models (compute frontier; aggregate across model configurations)
rows.operation_detail: Compare compute-frontier behavior above the sub-epoch regime
rows.measure: Change in compute-frontier scaling efficiency when examples are revisited
rows.value: The all-frontier exponent is −0.76; the paper describes diminishing returns after the frontier enters the multi-epoch regime
rows.note: The authors describe a potential shift in efficiency when compute is spent revisiting already-seen examples.
rows.check: This is a bend in the compute frontier once training enters multi-epoch, a V7 effect. It does not measure allocation, so drop V3. The V5 repeated-data limit is better carried by r14.

conditions.value: head dimensionality varied within the explored range

rows.measure: Effect of head dimensionality on minimum validation loss
rows.value: Head dimensionality did not significantly impact minimum training loss within the explored range
rows.note: The paper describes the effect as not significant within the tested range.
rows.check: The evidence is weak. The text cites the 'left panel of Fig. 4', but head dimensionality is the right panel, and Fig. 4 is a learning-rate-stability sweep. No loss numbers are given.

source_check.correct: Section 3.3 reports no significant effect of head dimensionality on minimum training loss. The row's operation and measure instead specify validation loss. Figure 4 labels its metric validation MSE and places the head variation in the right panel, although Section 3.3 cites the left panel. No numerical loss difference is stated.

rows.subject: TransformerPayne models (varying parameter-token count)
rows.operation_detail: Vary parameter-token count and compare performance relative to parameter count
rows.measure: Validation MSE improvement relative to parameter count
rows.value: Increasing token count is substantially less parameter-efficient than adjusting depth or width
rows.note: The text reports relative parameter efficiency rather than a numerical loss difference.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.3 final paragraph; Figure 5 caption; Appendix B and Figure B1 caption.

rows.subject: TransformerPayne models (aggregate over dataset sizes and model configurations)
rows.operation_detail: Compare performance when training examples are revisited across dataset-size conditions
rows.measure: Validation MSE as training proceeds and examples are revisited
rows.value: Performance continues to improve after multiple passes with diminishing returns; smaller datasets show saturation, and largest models on smaller datasets can plateau or increase in MSE
rows.locator: Sections 3.4.2–3.4.3 and Appendix B; Figure B3
rows.note: The authors report overfitting for the largest models on smaller datasets and state that smaller-dataset frontiers increasingly deviate from the initial scaling trends.
rows.check: Fine. Smaller datasets saturate and the largest models overfit (MSE plateaus or rises), so the power-law form does not continue under heavy data repetition.
